task: buy a physical product on Amazon: search for an item, work the results list, open and assess a product page (price, rating, variant options, delivery date), add to cart, and check out; complete when the order confirmation or the final checkout review screen with the order total is on screen. Surface pinned: Amazon's own website or app — not a third-party wrapper or assistive shopping app, not a haul/unboxing video, not a deals-roundup or affiliate-listicle without a live purchase session. Variants: returns and refunds (see returns), reordering a past purchase (see reorder), leaving a review (see review), and Amazon Fresh grocery orders (see groceries) do not belong.

tree.label: Buy a product on Amazon
tree.note: do 1. 2 before 3 when the wallet is funded up front (1sv0) - 7 reaches back into 2.3 to 2.6 when a gift card or shortfall surfaces at payment (BWIx). repeat 3 and 4 until the user settles on an item; 4.8 loops back to 3 for the next item when the order takes several (x0cE, 7wsx). then 5. 6 and 7 in the order the route dictates: cart paths meet 6 first (x0cE, 7wsx), buy-now paths land on 7 with the address riding on the same screen (bNZA, BKI3, BWIx). then 8; 8.6 to 8.8 only when the instrument demands an external authorization (x0cE, BKI3). 9 once the order exists - seven keepers do it in-video.

children.label: Get into Amazon
children.note: 1.1 then 1.2, with 1.10 on a first run before anything else. 1.3 and 1.4 as prompts and cross-border needs arise - 1.3 can fire mid-task too, gating whatever needed the permission (DLy4). then 1.5 to 1.9 as the account state demands - three keepers arrive signed in and skip all of it, and DLy4 skips sign-in outright.

questions.question: Is the shipping destination shown in the site's banner the one this order actually ships to?
questions.why: Verifying the 'Deliver to Malaysia' banner and account greeting ensures that product availability and shipping costs will be accurate for your location.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to verify that the agent is using your preferred account and regional settings before it starts filtering products.
questions.check: What location does the 'Deliver to' banner show, and does it match the delivery address in the task?
questions.say_example: The page says it's delivering to <another country>. Your order goes to <your address>, so I'm fixing that before we look at prices.

questions.question: Which search result is the correct Amazon app to select?
questions.why: The screen showed a sponsored third-party app at the top of the results, requiring you to bypass it and identify the official Amazon app to continue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to ensure the agent selects the legitimate Amazon application rather than a sponsored ad.
questions.check: Which results are marked Sponsored or Ad, and which result's developer or site name is Amazon's own?
questions.say_example: The first result is an ad for a different app. The real Amazon one is just below it, so that's the one I'm opening.

questions.question: Is the app being opened Amazon's own listing for your region, and not a lookalike?
questions.why: The Play Store search results display an 'Open' button next to 'Amazon India Shop, Pay, miniTV', confirming the app is already installed and ready to launch.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that the correct regional version of the Amazon app is being opened for the purchase.
questions.check: Does the store listing show an 'Open' button, meaning the app is already installed?
questions.say_example: Amazon was already installed, so I opened it.

questions.question: Should the app get the device permission it is asking for, and should that answer be remembered?
questions.why: The app requests camera access to scan barcodes or products and offers a checkbox to remember your permission choice for the future.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose direct control over your device's privacy settings and whether the app receives temporary or permanent camera access.
questions.verify_form: The agent answered the camera-permission prompt - check what it granted and whether it ticked the remember-this-choice box; that box makes the access permanent, not one-time.
questions.check: Does the page show a device permission prompt, which permission does it name, and is there a remember-this-choice checkbox?
questions.say_example: The app wants to use your camera. I said no, we don't need it to shop. And I left the remember box unticked.

questions.question: Should you allow the browser to save your login information?
questions.why: The browser prompt offers options to save, ignore, or password-protect your credentials, which dictates how securely your account is accessed in the future.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally decide your preferred balance between security and convenience for storing sensitive passwords.
questions.verify_form: The agent answered the browser's save-password prompt - check which option it took; saved, your login sits in this browser for anyone who opens it next.
questions.check: Does the page show a prompt offering to save the password, with save, never, or not-now options?
questions.say_example: The browser offered to remember your Amazon password. I said no. Your password stays with you.

questions.question: Do you want to change the delivery location to a US zip code to see all items, or keep it as your actual location?
questions.why: The "Choose your location" popup lets you enter a US zip code or select a country, which determines whether you see the full catalog or only items that ship to your specific region.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether to browse the complete US inventory or strictly filter for products that can be delivered to your international address.
questions.verify_form: The agent answered the 'Choose your location' popup - check whether it set a US zip to see the full catalog or kept your real address; that choice decided which items and shipping costs u were ever shown.
questions.check: What location or zip code does the 'Choose your location' popup show as selected?
questions.say_example: Kept delivery set to your real address, so everything you heard about ships to you.

questions.question: Should you sign in to your account before starting your search?
questions.why: The homepage displays a 'Sign in' button under the Account & Lists menu, which determines whether the purchase will be linked to an existing profile with saved payment and shipping details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing control over which specific Amazon account is used for the purchase, potentially resulting in the use of incorrect payment methods or shipping addresses.
questions.verify_form: The agent decided whether to sign in before searching - check whether the session is on your account or signed out; signed out it cannot see your saved addresses, payment methods, or Prime pricing.
questions.check: Does the header show 'Sign in' or an account greeting?
questions.say_example: Signed in first, so your addresses and your prices load from the start.

questions.question: Are you signed into the correct Amazon account?
questions.why: Checking the 'Hello, johnsavvy' greeting in the top right corner ensures the purchase will be billed to and tracked under the intended user profile.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the peace of mind of personally confirming that their own account, rather than a shared or incorrect one, is being used for the transaction.
questions.check: What name does the 'Hello, <name>' greeting in the header show?
questions.say_example: The page greets <a name that isn't yours>. Wrong account, so I'm signing out before anything goes in a cart.

questions.question: Which account should you log into, or should you create a new one?
questions.why: The login screen displays an autocomplete dropdown with multiple saved emails and a button for new customers, requiring a choice of which profile to use for the order.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide which specific account's payment methods and order history are used for this purchase.
questions.verify_form: The agent signed in with one of the saved emails or created a new account - check which; that account's cards and order history are what fund and record this purchase.
questions.check: Which saved emails does the sign-in screen's autocomplete list?
questions.say_example: The sign-in page remembers more than one account. I'll use <the one your task names>. OK, or pick a different one?

questions.question: What name and password will you use to register your new account?
questions.why: The registration form requires a name, email confirmation, and a new password to create an account and proceed with the checkout.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to choose the specific name and secure password associated with your new shopping account.
questions.verify_form: The agent registered the account with a name and password it chose - get both from it now; without that password the account, and any order inside it, is locked to you.
questions.check: Does the page show a create-account form asking for name, email, and password?
questions.say_example: This needs a brand-new account, and the password has to be yours, not mine. Can you set one, or is there an account I should sign in to instead?

questions.question: Are your registration details complete and correct before creating the account?
questions.why: Verifying that the name, email, and password fields are filled correctly ensures the account can be created without errors to proceed with checkout.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that their personal information and chosen password were typed correctly for their new account.
questions.check: Are the name and email fields filled, and does the email shown match the one in the task?
questions.say_example: The form has your email with one letter off. Fixing it, or the confirmation mail never reaches you.

questions.question: Will you use your mobile number or your email address to log in?
questions.why: The sign-in screen requires entering either a mobile number or an email address in the text field to continue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over which personal contact method and associated account is used for the transaction.
questions.verify_form: The agent signed in with either your mobile number or your email - check which it used; each maps to a different contact channel and possibly a different account.
questions.check: Does the sign-in field accept an email or a phone number, and which was entered?
questions.say_example: Signed in with your email.

questions.question: Checkout is asking for your password again - is it your account being re-authenticated, and does the sign-in go through?
questions.why: The 'Iniciar sesión' page requires you to re-enter your password to verify your identity before allowing you to continue to checkout.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the security of keeping your password private, as the agent would need your exact credentials to bypass this authentication step.
questions.check: Does the page ask for the password to be entered again before continuing?
questions.say_example: Amazon wants your password again before it takes the order. That field is yours. I'll wait.

questions.question: Is the email shown on the password screen the account you meant to use?
questions.why: Verifying the displayed email '[email]' and entering the correct password ensures you are accessing the right account to complete the purchase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify that the purchase is being made under their preferred account.
questions.check: What email does the password page display above the password field?
questions.say_example: The password box is for <a different email> than the account you named. Stopping the sign-in before it lands in the wrong account.

questions.question: Which language do you prefer for the app interface?
questions.why: The screen presents multiple language options like English, Hindi, and Tamil, determining the language used for all subsequent navigation and product details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to set the app to their preferred native language for a more comfortable shopping experience.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the app language from the English/Hindi/Tamil screen - check which one it picked; every menu and product page from here on renders in it.
questions.check: Which language options does the screen list, and which one is selected?
questions.say_example: Kept the app in <your language>.

children.label: Fund the balance
children.note: 2.1 then 2.2 on the hub route (1sv0); 7.4 enters directly at 2.3 mid-checkout (BWIx). 2.4 after any addition; 2.5 and 2.6 only when the balance falls short of the order.

questions.question: Are you entering the correct gift card code to add to your balance?
questions.why: Verifying the exact code ensures the funds are successfully added to your existing ₹9570.25 balance.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to personally verify that the correct gift card code is being applied to their account.
questions.check: Does the code typed in the entry field match the string the voucher screen labels as the gift card or claim code, not the transaction ID?
questions.say_example: The code in the box doesn't match the one on your voucher. One block is off, so I'm re-entering it before applying.

questions.question: Did the balance go up by exactly the gift card's value?
questions.why: Confirming that the ₹200.00 gift card correctly updated the initial ₹30.01 balance to ₹230.01 ensures you are receiving the exact credit expected before paying.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance of personally verifying that the gift card funds were accurately calculated and applied to their account balance.
questions.check: What were the balance before, the gift card value, and the balance after, as shown on screen?
questions.say_example: The card was <200> but the balance only went up <150>. Those should match. Holding here until we know where the rest went.

questions.question: Did the gift card money land in your balance?
questions.why: Confirming the success message and updated balance ensures your funds were applied correctly, and checking the statement verifies the transaction details.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of seeing your updated balance and the ability to personally verify the transaction history.
questions.check: Does the page show a success message and the updated balance?
questions.say_example: The gift card went through. Your balance is now <230>.

questions.question: Does your Amazon Pay balance at checkout match the amount confirmed earlier?
questions.why: The available balance at checkout shows ₹11,978.07, which contradicts the ₹[number].25 balance confirmed just after adding the gift card.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses financial transparency and trust in the transaction if the agent ignores an unexplained discrepancy in their funds.
questions.check: What balance does this screen show, and what did the last screen that showed the balance say?
questions.say_example: The balance here reads <a hundred more> than it did a minute ago. I want to know why before we spend from it.

children.label: Pick the top-up amount and method

questions.question: Your balance cannot cover the order - do you top it up via 'Add Now' or switch to another payment method?
questions.why: The screen displays an insufficient balance warning with an 'Add Now' button, requiring a decision on how to cover the remaining cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to control exactly how much money is added to their account balance or whether to use an alternative payment method.
questions.verify_form: The agent either topped up your balance via Add Now or switched payment methods - check which, and if it topped up, how much it moved into the balance; that money leaves your bank either way.
questions.check: Does the page show an insufficient-balance warning, the shortfall amount, and an 'Add Now' option?
questions.say_example: Your balance is <57> short of the total. I can top it up from your bank, or charge the rest to your card. Which?

questions.question: Does the top-up match the shortfall, or does it park extra money in the balance?
questions.why: Verifying the math ensures the ₹57.03 top-up exactly covers the shortfall between the ₹287.04 product price and the ₹230.01 available balance shown on screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the financial oversight of confirming that only the exact required amount is being added to their account.
questions.check: What are the product total, the available balance, and the top-up amount shown on screen?
questions.say_example: The top-up it suggests is more than the gap. That parks extra money in the balance, so I'm topping up just the difference.

children.label: Authorize the top-up in the payment app
Find the product
children.note: one of 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, or 3.5 to raise candidates - 3.2 rides on 3.1. then 3.6, with 3.7 running wherever ads sit in the list. re-entered per item on multi-item orders.

questions.question: Are you sure this is the correct wishlist link to open?
questions.why: Navigating directly to the specific wishlist URL ensures you are selecting the exact pre-approved items without having to search for them manually.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the guarantee that the agent is purchasing from their specifically curated wishlist rather than relying on a generic search.
questions.check: Whose name and which list title does the wishlist page header show, and do they match the list named in the task?
questions.say_example: This list belongs to <a different name> than the one in your task. Finding the right one before picking anything.

questions.question: Does the wish list continue below the current view, with saved items not yet on screen?
questions.why: Exploring further down the list reveals previously saved options like the Saucony socks and PUMA running shoes, allowing for a broader comparison before deciding.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally rediscover and evaluate older saved items that might better suit your current needs than the top results.
questions.check: Does the list show more items below the current view, or a load-more control?
questions.say_example: Read the whole list, all <12> items, before comparing.

questions.question: When were these items originally added to your list?
questions.why: Checking the 'added on' dates shown on the screen helps you evaluate if the items are still relevant to your current needs.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the personal context of knowing how long an item has been saved and whether your desire for it has faded over time.
questions.verify_form: The agent shopped from items saved long ago - check the 'added on' dates of what it picked; only u know whether something saved months back is still wanted.
questions.check: What 'added on' dates does the list show beside each item?
questions.say_example: The pick was saved to the list <two years> ago, in case that changes anything. It's in the report.

questions.question: Which department should you select from the dropdown to narrow your search?
questions.why: Selecting a specific category from the dropdown, such as 'Electronics & Photo' or 'Books', prevents irrelevant results from other departments from cluttering your search.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to intuitively narrow the search scope based on their personal understanding of which department best fits the desired item.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a department from the search dropdown - check whether the one it chose, like Electronics & Photo or Books, actually covers the item; the wrong department hides every right result.
questions.check: Which department is selected in the search dropdown?
questions.say_example: Searched inside <Electronics> so the results stay on topic.

questions.question: What should you do when your uploaded photo doesn't appear in the visual search?
questions.why: The screen displayed a default image instead of the selected plant photo, indicating the upload failed and an alternative method like the live camera was needed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to troubleshoot the failed image upload and manually decide how to capture the item's visual information.
questions.verify_form: The upload failed and a default image loaded instead of the plant photo - the agent picked a recovery on its own; check whether it retried the upload, switched to the live camera, or searched something else entirely.
questions.check: Does the visual search show the uploaded photo, or a default or placeholder image in its place?
questions.say_example: Your photo didn't upload - the search ran on a placeholder, so these matches mean nothing. Trying the upload again.

questions.question: Which of these results should I pick?
questions.why: The search results display a mix of sponsored items, best sellers, and combo packs with varying prices and ratings, requiring you to weigh these factors to find the right match.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might default to the first sponsored result or best seller instead of scrolling to find a combo pack that better aligns with your specific style and value preferences.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a t-shirt from a page mixing sponsored items, best sellers, and combo packs - check what it chose and what it passed over; the default failure is taking the first sponsored result instead of the combo pack that better fits your style and budget.
questions.check: Which results are shown, with title, price, rating, review count, and any Sponsored tag?
questions.say_example: Three that fit. The <first> at <12>, rated <4.6> by <two thousand> people. The <second> at <9>, fewer reviews. The <third> is a two-pack at <15>. Which one?

questions.question: Is that huge discount real, or is the 'was' price just the seller's own claim?
questions.why: The search results show multiple options with varying ratings, review counts, and massive discounts like the 93% off Fire-Boltt, requiring a careful comparison to find the best value.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply your personal preferences regarding brand trust, aesthetic appeal, and skepticism toward heavily discounted sponsored items when choosing which product to investigate further.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked a smartwatch from results full of steep sponsored discounts - check what it chose and whether it bought the 93%-off Fire-Boltt discount story; only u can weigh brand trust against a too-good number.
questions.check: What discount percentage and struck-through reference price does the listing show?
questions.say_example: That one says <93> percent off. The old price is the seller's own claim, not something the site checked, so judge it by the <7 dollar> price, not the discount.

children.label: Tell the ads from the results

questions.question: Do you select the first sponsored result or scroll down to compare with organic listings?
questions.why: The top result is a sponsored listing for the Meta Quest 3 at $499.00, and organic results might offer better prices or alternative bundles.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to find a better deal or a more suitable bundle by not reviewing all available search results.
questions.verify_form: The top result was a sponsored Meta Quest 3 at $499.00 - check whether the agent took it or scrolled to the organic listings; the sponsored slot is bought, not earned, and a cheaper bundle may sit below it.
questions.check: Which of the top results are labeled Sponsored, and what organic results sit below them?
questions.say_example: The top result is an ad. The same thing sits lower without the badge, so I'm comparing both before picking.

children.label: Vet the item
children.note: 4.1 to 4.6 in any order and depth - the corpus mostly reads 4.1 and skips 4.3. 4.7 whenever the item has variants; 4.8 and 4.9 where formats and fit make it matter. 4.7 re-prices the page, so 4.5 and 4.6 are re-read after it.

questions.question: Does the product page still show the item, price, and date you agreed to?
questions.why: This matters because you need to confirm that the selected variant, such as the Black color, and the deal price of ₹ 5,299.00 meet your preferences before proceeding.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to personally evaluate and choose between different color variants based on their own aesthetic preferences.
questions.verify_form: The agent settled on the Black variant at the ₹5,299 deal price - check the color against what you actually wanted; the other colorways sat on the same page, and this is the one that ships.
questions.check: Do the variant, price, and delivery date now shown on the product page match what the person approved at the pick?
questions.say_example: The page now shows <a different color> at <a higher price> than the one you said yes to. Squaring that before it goes in the cart.

questions.question: Do you want to use a third-party freight forwarder since this item doesn't ship directly to your location?
questions.why: The screen explicitly states that the item does not ship to Malaysia, meaning an alternative shipping method must be arranged to complete the purchase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether the extra cost and hassle of setting up a freight forwarder are worth it for this specific product.
questions.verify_form: The item doesn't ship to Malaysia, and the agent decided how to handle that - check whether it committed to a freight forwarder or dropped the item; only you can say if the forwarder's extra cost and handling is worth it for this product.
questions.check: Does the page state that the item does not ship to the selected address or country?
questions.say_example: This one won't ship to <your country>. A forwarding service could relay it, but that's extra cost, extra weeks, and an account you'd have to set up. Want that, or should I find one that ships direct?

questions.question: Which brand is the old phone you are trading in?
questions.why: Selecting the correct brand from the list ensures you receive the accurate trade-in value for your specific device.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to specify exactly which old device they are trading in, potentially resulting in an incorrect discount or a rejected exchange.
questions.verify_form: The agent declared your old phone's brand to the trade-in wizard - only you know what's actually in your drawer; a wrong brand means the doorstep inspector rejects the exchange and the discount vanishes.
questions.check: Does the page show the trade-in wizard asking for the device's brand, model, storage, condition, or IMEI?
questions.say_example: The trade-in wants facts about the phone in your hand - brand, model, storage, condition, its IMEI. I can't answer those, and a wrong answer kills the credit at the doorstep. Take these few questions, or skip the trade-in?

questions.question: Is your old phone's IMEI verified, and are you ready for the condition test?
questions.why: The green checkmark confirms your specific device is eligible for the exchange offer up to ₹6500 before you initiate the required diagnostic test.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of personally verifying that your exact old phone was accepted for the trade-in value.
questions.check: Does the page show the IMEI accepted and the exchange eligibility confirmed?
questions.say_example: Your phone passed the IMEI check. The exchange credit shows <6,500>.

questions.question: Do you check the customer reviews and ratings to verify the product quality?
questions.why: Although the screen displays the manufacturer's material and care details, checking the reviews tab reveals actual customer experiences with the item.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally weigh the customer feedback and decide if the product's real-world quality meets your specific standards.
questions.verify_form: The agent judged the product from the listing's own details - the review tab with real customer experiences went unread. Only you can say whether stranger feedback matters for this buy; if it does, open the reviews before the order, not after the package arrives.
questions.check: What rating, review count, and top review excerpts does the page show?
questions.say_example: Read the reviews. The repeated complaint is <the strap breaking>, worth knowing before it ships.

questions.question: How many people is this rating actually based on?
questions.why: The screen shows a 4-star rating but notes there are only two customer reviews, meaning the rating might not be a reliable indicator of quality.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to read the specific reviews and decide for yourself if the limited feedback justifies the purchase.
questions.verify_form: The agent treated the 4-star badge as good enough - it rests on exactly two reviews; only you can say whether two strangers' opinions clear your bar, and two reviews is few enough to read yourself before buying.
questions.check: What rating does the page show, and from how many reviews?
questions.say_example: It's rated <4 stars>, but that's from just <2> people. Thin ground. Both are short enough to read out, want them?

questions.question: Does the number of ratings on the product page match what you saw in the search results?
questions.why: The search results displayed 12,534 ratings for the Bare Home Fleece Blanket, but the product detail page shows 12,392 ratings.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to notice discrepancies in product metrics that could indicate a glitch or an unexpected change in the selected item variation.
questions.check: What rating counts do the search result and the product page each show?
questions.say_example: The listing's review count differs slightly from the search page. Logged it, it's usually just the site's own lag.

questions.question: Is this sold by Amazon, or by a third-party seller you'd have to trust?
questions.why: The screen displays specific fulfillment details like "Sold by Clicktech Retail Private Ltd" and a "1 Year Warranty" that determine the reliability and protection of your purchase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally vet the third-party seller and confirm the warranty terms before committing to the checkout process.
questions.verify_form: The agent proceeded with 'Sold by Clicktech Retail Private Ltd' - a third party, not Amazon - check the seller's record and who actually issues the 1-year warranty; the seller you accept is who you'll chase when something breaks.

children.label: Decide whether to save the card

questions.question: Do you want to save this credit card for future purchases?
questions.why: The payment screen includes a checkbox to save your card details per RBI guidelines, which affects your account's stored financial data.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose control over your financial privacy and security if the agent decides whether to permanently store your credit card information on the platform.
questions.verify_form: The agent set the save-this-card checkbox one way or the other - check which; ticked, your card number lives on the platform for every future session the agent runs.
questions.check: Is the save-this-card checkbox ticked?
questions.say_example: Didn't save the card to the account - it was used for this order only.

questions.question: Do you want to use your available gift card and promotional balances to cover the entire order?
questions.why: The order summary showed a total of $73.88, which could be fully covered by the selected $75.58 gift card and $7.00 promotional balances without charging your Mastercard.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to spend your existing gift card balance now or save it for a future purchase and charge the credit card instead.
questions.verify_form: The agent decided how to fund the $73.88 order - check whether it spent the $75.58 gift card and $7.00 promotional balance or charged the Mastercard; spending the balances now means they're gone for whatever you were saving them for.
questions.check: What gift card, promotional, or points balances does the page show as available, and are they selected?
questions.say_example: Your gift card balance covers this whole order, so the card wouldn't be charged at all. Spend the balance here, or save it and use the card?

children.label: Review and place the order
children.note: 8.1 with 8.2 against it; 8.3 where a code exists; 8.4 before 8.5 where the platform shows terms. 8.5 commits - except on external instruments, where 8.6 to 8.8 finish it on the bank's pages (x0cE, BKI3), and on the points detour, where the commit button lives on the payment screen itself and no recalculated total is ever shown (RJe-).

questions.question: Is this delivery fee worth it, given it eats the discount?
questions.why: The checkout screen shows a $19.99 arranged delivery fee for the chair, which completely offsets the $4.00 discount and significantly increases the final cost.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether the unexpected delivery fee makes this specific item too expensive compared to alternatives with free shipping.
questions.verify_form: The agent accepted the $19.99 arranged delivery fee on the chair - that fee wipes out the $4.00 discount and then some; check whether the chair is still worth it against a free-shipping alternative.
questions.check: Does the summary show a delivery, convenience, or handling fee that was not part of the item price, and how large is it against any discounts?
questions.say_example: A <19.99> delivery fee just attached to the chair - it eats the whole <4 dollar> discount and more. Keep the chair, or drop it?

children.label: Check the totals and dates against the earlier screens

questions.question: Did any item's price change while it sat in the cart?
questions.why: The Moto E was priced at ₹5,299.00 when added, but the final two-item subtotal of ₹11,198.00 shows it dropped to ₹4,999.00.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to accurately track their expected spending if the agent ignores spontaneous price changes in the cart.
questions.check: Does any cart or checkout line show a different price for an item than the price at which it was added?
questions.say_example: Heads up - the phone got cheaper while it sat in the cart, <5,299> down to <4,999>. The total uses the lower one.

questions.question: Does the promised delivery date stay consistent from the product page all the way through checkout?
questions.why: Confirming that the delivery date promised on the product page matches the final checkout screen ensures you are not surprised by unexpected shipping delays.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to catch last-minute shipping changes that might silently appear before finalizing the order.
questions.check: What delivery date did the product page promise, and what date does each later screen, through confirmation, show?
questions.say_example: The listing said <Friday>, but checkout now says <next Tuesday>. If the date was the point, this is the moment to change course.

questions.question: Did the coupon you saw in the cart actually apply to your final total?
questions.why: Checking that the promised $4.00 coupon from the cart appears as a -$4.00 deduction in the order summary ensures the discount was honored.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the financial oversight of confirming that promised discounts were actually applied to your final bill.
questions.check: Which coupons, promotional balances, or points were clipped or selected earlier, and does the final summary show each as a deduction?
questions.say_example: The <4 dollar> coupon from the cart isn't in the final total. Not paying full price silently - fixing it before the order.

questions.question: Does the checkout total match the price you saw on the product page?
questions.why: The checkout screen demands ₹60,225.00 instead of the ₹53,720 shown on the product page, indicating a significant unexpected price increase.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses financial control and ends up paying significantly more than the expected price.
questions.check: For each money line - total, shipping, fees, savings - what did the earlier screen promise and what does this screen charge?
questions.say_example: Checkout wants <60,225>, but the page you approved said <53,720>. That's <6,505> more with nothing on screen explaining it. Holding until it's accounted for.

questions.question: Does the final order total correctly account for the item price, fees, and applied discounts?
questions.why: Verifying the math ensures the final total correctly applies the expected delivery discount and cash on delivery fee to the base item price.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the financial oversight of personally confirming that all expected discounts were applied and no unexpected fees were added before placing the order.
questions.check: Do the item prices, fees, and deductions listed on the final summary sum to the total shown?
questions.say_example: The pieces on screen add to <501.90> but the total says <520.81>. The extra <18.91> has no label. Holding the order until it does.

questions.question: Is the delivery estimate far enough out to change your mind?
questions.why: The screen displays an estimated delivery date of '6 Jan 2026', meaning you would be waiting years for the item to arrive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to catch and cancel an order with an unacceptable multi-year delivery delay.
questions.verify_form: The agent went ahead despite the '6 Jan 2026' delivery estimate - confirm you actually accept a multi-year wait; this was the moment to cancel, not after the charge.
questions.check: What estimated delivery date does the order screen show, and how far out is it?
questions.say_example: Before anything is placed - the delivery estimate is <months> out, <January>, not this week. Still want it?

questions.question: Ready to place this order?
questions.why: The checkout screen prompts for a payment method and shows a $172.41 total, which must be submitted to actually place the order.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the actual purchase of the items because the agent falsely claims the order is complete without ever submitting payment.
questions.check: What do the order screen's final lines show - items, quantities, variant, address, payment method, total, and any cancellation terms?
questions.say_example: Ready to order. <The kettle>, one, to <Home>, arriving <Friday>. <21.40> total on <your Mastercard ending 9034>. Cancelling stays free until it ships. Press to order, or say change.

questions.question: Do you want to grant Amazon permission to read your text messages to automatically fill the OTP?
questions.why: The app explicitly requests SMS access to auto-read OTPs, requiring a choice between checkout convenience and message privacy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to decide whether to protect their SMS privacy or grant the app access for convenience.
questions.verify_form: The agent answered the SMS-permission prompt - check which way; granted, the app reads your text messages from now on, well beyond this one OTP.
questions.check: Does the app show a prompt asking for SMS or message access to auto-fill codes?
questions.say_example: The app asked to read your texts so it can grab the code itself. I said no - that access outlives this one code. The code box is yours.

questions.question: How do you complete the bank's two-factor authentication?
questions.why: The Federal Bank authentication page requires a secret SMS OTP to securely authorize the payment.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses full automation because the agent cannot access the SMS OTP sent to their personal phone to authorize the payment.
questions.check: Does the page show a one-time-code entry field for the bank's verification?
questions.say_example: Your bank sent a code to your phone. Only you have it. The box is ready when you are.

children.label: Verify the order
children.note: 9.1, then 9.2 as the upsells land; 9.3 to 9.5 in order. seven keepers run it; x0cE tracks an older order instead of the new one.

questions.question: Did the order actually go through?
questions.why: Confirming the 'Order placed' message and the delivery date ensures the transaction went through and the item will arrive when expected.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate peace of mind of seeing the confirmation screen and knowing exactly when their item will arrive.
questions.check: Does the page show an order-placed confirmation, an order number, and a delivery date?
questions.say_example: Order's in. The confirmation is on screen, arriving <Friday>, and cancelling stays free until it ships.

questions.question: Does the confirmation email reflect the correct delivery dates and a zero total balance?
questions.why: Checking the email ensures that the gift card fully covered the CDN$ 0.00 total and that the delivery dates for the split shipments are accurate.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the peace of mind of personally verifying that no unexpected charges were made and knowing exactly when each part of the order will arrive.
questions.check: Does the confirmation email list the same items, dates, and total as the order screen?
questions.say_example: The confirmation email came, and it matches what you approved. That email is your proof rather than my word.

questions.question: Do you open the newly placed order in your order history to verify its details?
questions.why: Checking the order history confirms that the purchase went through successfully and displays the current dispatch status and estimated delivery date.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of seeing the order successfully logged in your account with its confirmed delivery timeline.
questions.check: Does the orders page list this order with its status and delivery estimate?
questions.say_example: It's in your orders too - status <Ordered>, arriving <Friday>.

questions.question: What is the current tracking status and expected delivery date for your order?
questions.why: The screen displays the order tracking timeline, confirming the order was placed today and showing when it will arrive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The person loses the immediate reassurance of seeing the confirmed order status and knowing exactly when it will arrive.
questions.check: What status and delivery estimate does the tracking timeline show?
questions.say_example: Tracking shows <Ordered> as of today, arriving <Friday>.
